extracted.intended_audience: scientists, researchers, and science communicators planning public engagement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and delivering public engagement about scientific work, using a goal–audience–message framework to define objectives, identify and analyze audiences, craft memorable messages, and avoid jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: goal-audience-message framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful engagement builds on a foundation of clear, concise communication. Remember the framework of goal-audience-message when thinking about how to communicate about your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this three-part framework to align your objectives (what you want to achieve), your chosen audience (who can help you achieve it), and your message (what you want them to hear and remember). The rest of the toolkit provides specific tactics that apply within this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: define communication goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Public engagement with science starts with a goal in mind; goals may be long-term (e.g., fostering trust, improving use of scientific evidence) or shorter-term (e.g., increasing interest in a topic, humanizing scientists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific outcomes you want from an engagement. Consider both long-term systemic outcomes and actionable short-term targets; focusing on a few specific goals (often shorter-term) can make your strategy more practical and measurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: focus on short-term, specific outcomes when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Your engagement strategy may have a few specific goals in mind; consider focusing on shorter-term outcomes, such as increasing interest in a particular topic or 'humanizing' scientists and science, which can later lead to longer-term goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term, concrete outcomes can be stepping stones toward broader aims. Make those outcomes explicit so you can tailor message and tactics and evaluate success.

rubrics_metrics.name: select and define target audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: You can choose to focus your communication on the audiences that are best-positioned to help you reach your communication goals. Clearly define your audience and consider groups with which you already have connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting audiences, ask: What might the audience be interested in related to my topic? What commonalities do I have with the audience? What questions might the audience ask? Prioritize audiences whose interests and influence align with your goals (e.g., decision-makers or their constituents).

rubrics_metrics.name: consider the venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you speaking at a science café, or planning a social media strategy? Reach out to the point of contact or organizer for information and to ask questions about the attendees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use venue information to tailor tone, depth, and format. For media interviews, ask the reporter about the story and the kind of information they want. Venue determines expectations, audience makeup, and appropriate message framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: research your audience and channels beforehand (conduct an internet search)
rubrics_metrics.description: What type of events has the organization held in the past? Read or watch some stories the journalist wrote or produced to determine their perspective on the topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review past content from organizers, journalists, or social media accounts of your target audience to understand interests, framing, and likely questions. Use that insight to align examples, language, and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: assess audience on the spot
rubrics_metrics.description: For in-person engagements, take some time beforehand to meet audience members. During an event, you can take a quick poll of the audience by asking for a show of hands, to get a sense of prior experience or interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quick, low-effort audience checks (meet-and-greet, hand-raise polls) to adapt depth and examples in real time. Meeting audience members beforehand helps you find commonalities to build rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: start with 'Why Should I Care?' (lead with the big picture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start out by communicating the 'big picture' and why the audience should care. Then go into an appropriate level of detail to emphasize your key points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with relevance and impact to capture attention. After the big-picture hook, provide supporting details tailored to the audience's interests and knowledge level.

rubrics_metrics.name: three-point message structure
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the three things you want your audience to remember and respond to? Organize your message around these key points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit your core message to three main takeaways (e.g., three research focuses, three results, three reasons the work matters). Use the three points as anchors you can return to; add detail as needed but keep the takeaways memorable. The AAAS 'What We Know' initiative is given as an example of summarizing large content into three memorable ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: choose key points based on audience needs
rubrics_metrics.description: How do you choose just three key points? Think about your audience and what they want to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick three points that align with the audience's interests, questions, and motivations. Examples include emphasizing practical applications, major findings, or reasons the work matters to that specific audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid and translate jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon can be, in my mind, a tool, a weapon, a wall, and/or a bridge. Jargon is important shorthand within a field, but that language can be used to keep others out, or to shut others down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that technical terms may confuse or alienate non-expert audiences (and even other scientists). Try language out on friends, family, and colleagues without the same technical background to learn which words work. Use plain-language alternatives (example: 'break open cells' instead of 'induce lysis') and iterate with feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: apply communication strategies and use visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: The other pages in this section provide guidance for applying the goal-audience-message framework to different communication channels and audiences, as well as tips for using visual communication throughout your various engagements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select channels and visual tools that suit your audience and goals. Use visuals to clarify complex information and reinforce the three key messages. Seek out additional resources (e.g., AAAS webinars and workshops) for channel-specific tactics.
